questions.q: Which set contains the three branches of the intermediate-mesoderm diagram?

Primitive rectum, anal pit, phallic urethra

questions.q: Which bud arises from the mesonephric duct in the diagram?

questions.q: The paramesonephric duct is also known as which duct?

questions.q: How does the text describe the swellings of the urogenital ridge?
opts: One unpaired swelling ventral to the heart
Three pairs beside the neural crest
Four pairs within the primitive gut
Two pairs, on either side of the dorsal aorta
questions.exp: The third bullet describes two pairs of swellings on either side of the dorsal aorta. (Book p706)

questions.q: Fill up: The medial swelling is the ______ ridge.
questions.exp: The medial swelling is named the genital ridge. (Book p706)

questions.q: Which pair of organs is linked to the genital ridge?
questions.exp: The arrow from the genital ridge leads to ovary and testis. (Book p706)

questions.q: The lateral swelling of the urogenital ridge is the:

questions.q: The appendix of the epididymis is a remnant of which duct?

questions.q: Which embryonic structure is identified as the kidney in the final note?

questions.q: On which day does the timeline place pronephros formation?

questions.q: What happens to the pronephros after its formation?
opts: It regresses in a few days
It persists as the adult kidney
questions.exp: The second event in the first row is regression in a few days. (Book p706)

questions.q: When does the timeline place formation of the mesonephros?
questions.exp: The second timeline row begins with mesonephros formation at the end of the fourth week. (Book p706)

questions.q: Fill up: The mesonephros regresses by ______ in the timeline.
questions.exp: The next mesonephros bullet gives regression by four months. (Book p706)

questions.q: Which qualification is essential when reading this timeline’s statement that the mesonephros has “no role in humans”?
opts: It is the book’s shorthand, not a denial of all transient embryonic roles
It proves the mesonephric duct has no human derivatives
It means human embryos never form a mesonephros
It establishes mesonephros as the permanent human kidney
questions.exp: The scan says “No role in humans.” Treat that as source wording, not a literal claim that the embryonic mesonephros or its duct has no developmental roles. The same page describes human mesonephric-duct derivatives. (Book p706)

questions.q: Which animals are named in the book’s parenthesis beside the mesonephros?
questions.exp: The printed parenthesis says “Kidney of amphibians, reptiles.” This records the source wording; it should not be generalized as a comparative-anatomy rule that adult reptiles lack a metanephros. (Book p706)

questions.q: In the fifth week, mesenchyme of the metanephric blastema forms from which structure?
questions.exp: The first fifth-week event is formation of mesenchyme of the metanephric blastema from the nephrogenic cord. (Book p706)

questions.q: In the fifth week, epithelium of the ureteric bud forms from which duct?
questions.exp: The second fifth-week event is formation of ureteric-bud epithelium from the mesonephric duct. (Book p706)

questions.q: During which weeks is epithelial–mesenchymal interaction/transition placed in the timeline?
questions.exp: The continuation table places epithelial–mesenchymal interaction/transition in weeks 6–8. (Book p707)

questions.q: Which two tissues participate in the interaction described for weeks 6–8?
questions.exp: The parenthesis names epithelium of the ureteric bud and mesenchyme of the metanephric bud. (Book p707)

questions.q: Fill up: WT1 is described as a ______.
questions.exp: The first WT1 sub-bullet identifies it as a transcription factor. (Book p707)

questions.q: On which chromosome is WT1 located?
questions.exp: The second WT1 sub-bullet specifies chromosome 11. (Book p707)

questions.q: When does the first fully formed nephron appear in the timeline?
questions.exp: The next row gives end of the eighth week for the first fully formed nephron. (Book p707)

questions.q: At which stage does urine formation by filtration begin in the table?
questions.exp: The first event at 9–10 weeks is formation of urine (filtration). (Book p707)

questions.q: Which movement of the kidney accompanies the 9–10-week stage?
questions.exp: The second event in the 9–10-week row is ascent of the kidney with rotation. (Book p707)

questions.q: Fill up: Nephrogenesis is completed at ______ gestational weeks.
questions.exp: The next row places completion of nephrogenesis at 32–36 weeks. (Book p707)

questions.q: What proportion of nephrons is formed in the third trimester?
questions.exp: The next bullet states that 60–70% of nephrons form in the third trimester. (Book p707)

questions.q: At birth, how is the number of nephrons described?
questions.exp: The at-birth row states fixed number of nephrons. (Book p707)

questions.q: Which statement about nephron formation after birth matches the table?
opts: No new nephron is formed or replaced
questions.exp: The first after-birth bullet states that no new nephron is formed or replaced. (Book p707)

questions.q: How does urine-concentrating capacity change after birth?
questions.exp: The final row shows an increase in urine concentration capacity after birth. (Book p707)

questions.q: By what age does urine-concentrating capacity reach the adult level?
questions.exp: The final arrow gives adult-level urine concentration capacity by 1.5 years. (Book p707)

questions.q: Fill up: The nephron-number defining parameter highlighted here is ______.
questions.exp: The line immediately under Pathogenesis of CKD identifies birth weight as the nephron-number defining parameter. (Book p707)

questions.q: In this flowchart, lower birth weight is linked first to which change?
questions.exp: The opening arrow connects reduced birth weight to a reduced number of functional nephrons. (Book p707)

questions.q: A patient born at low birth weight has fewer functional nephrons. Which compensatory change follows in the diagram?
questions.exp: The next arrow links fewer functional nephrons to increased single-nephron GFR. (Book p707)

questions.q: Total GFR equals single-nephron GFR multiplied by which quantity?
questions.exp: The parenthetical equation is GFR = single-nephron GFR × number of functional nephrons. It is tested at its printed position, before the downward cascade. (Book p707)

questions.q: What is the next labelled state beneath the GFR equation?
questions.exp: The downward arrow from increased single-nephron GFR leads to glomerular hyperfiltration. (Book p707)

questions.q: Glomerular hyperfiltration is followed by which pressure change?
questions.exp: The next arrow leads from glomerular hyperfiltration to intraglomerular hypertension. (Book p707)

questions.q: Fill up: Intraglomerular hypertension leads to ______ injury in the cascade.
questions.exp: The next labelled step is hyperfiltration injury. (Book p707)

questions.q: Which capillary-pore change immediately follows hyperfiltration injury?
questions.exp: The next arrow leads to stretching of the capillary pore. (Book p707)

questions.q: What happens to capillary-pore diameter after stretching?
questions.exp: The next step is increased diameter of the capillary pore. (Book p707)

questions.q: After increased capillary-pore diameter, which urinary abnormality is labelled in the flowchart?
questions.exp: The flowchart labels proteinuria. Its parenthesis reads “Albuminemia,” which refers to blood rather than urine and appears to be a wording error here; albumin in urine is albuminuria. The printed wording is flagged, not silently treated as correct terminology. (Book p707)

questions.q: Which injury directly follows proteinuria in the cascade?
questions.exp: The arrow from proteinuria leads to tubular injury. (Book p707)

questions.q: Which process follows tubular injury along the leftward arrow?
questions.exp: The lower flowchart turns left from tubular injury to interstitial inflammation. (Book p707)

questions.q: Fill up: Interstitial inflammation is followed by release of ______.
questions.exp: The next leftward arrow leads to TGF-β release. (Book p707)

questions.q: Which two compartments undergo fibrosis after TGF-β release?
questions.exp: The upward arrow from TGF-β release leads to fibrosis of tubules and interstitium. (Book p707)

questions.q: What is the final disease endpoint of this fibrosis cascade?
questions.exp: The final upward arrow ends at CKD. (Book p707)

questions.q: The first CKD feature on this page is a reduction in what?
questions.exp: The opening CKD-features bullet describes a decrease in the number of functional nephrons. (Book p708)

questions.q: Which interstitial change is included in the listed CKD features?
questions.exp: The second CKD-features bullet first names interstitial fibrosis. (Book p708)

questions.q: Fill up: The tubular change paired with interstitial fibrosis is tubular ______.
questions.exp: The next component in the CKD-features line is tubular atrophy. (Book p708)

questions.q: Which glomerular change completes the CKD-features line?
questions.exp: The line ends with glomerulosclerosis. No numerical percentage is supplied in the scan. (Book p708)

questions.q: Which maternal condition follows “age of conception” in the diagram?
questions.exp: The diagram begins age of conception → pre-eclampsia/hypertension. It gives no age threshold and should not be read as an inevitable outcome at any particular age. (Book p708)

questions.q: Which placental problem follows maternal pre-eclampsia/hypertension?
questions.exp: The next arrow leads to placental insufficiency. (Book p708)

questions.q: Placental insufficiency is followed by which fetal growth problem?
questions.exp: The printed term is intra-uterine growth retardation (IUGR), commonly termed intrauterine growth restriction. (Book p708)

questions.q: Fill up: The next outcome after IUGR in the diagram is a ______ baby.
questions.exp: The next box is small for gestational age (SGA) baby. (Book p708)

questions.q: Which renal risk is listed for the small-for-gestational-age offspring?

questions.q: Which blood-pressure disorder is listed as an increased risk for these offspring?

questions.q: Which urate-related abnormality is included in the risk list?

questions.q: Which glucose-metabolism disorder is included in the offspring risk list?

questions.q: Which syndrome completes the list of increased risks after SGA birth?

questions.q: Fill up: ______ is important for formation of the epithelium of the ureteric bud.

questions.q: What vertebral range is listed for the adult kidney?
questions.exp: The adult-kidney location is T12–L3. (Book p708)

questions.q: What vertebral range is listed for the fetal kidney?

questions.q: WAGR is introduced under mutation of which gene?
questions.exp: The heading WT1 Gene Mutation is followed by WAGR mutation. (Book p708)

questions.q: Which renal tumour forms the W component of WAGR?

questions.q: A child with WAGR has the eye abnormality illustrated in the second panel. Which abnormality is named?
questions.exp: The second photograph is captioned aniridia. (Book p708)

questions.exp: The third figure caption is genitourinary abnormalities. (Book p708)

questions.q: Which tumour is the first feature illustrated for Denys–Drash syndrome?

questions.q: Which glomerular lesion is illustrated for Denys–Drash syndrome?

questions.q: How does this book’s Frasier diagram describe external genitalia?
questions.exp: The third gonadal bullet says external genitalia normal. This is the source’s description, not a universal exclusion of sex-development differences in every patient with Frasier syndrome. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which biopsy lesion is listed for Frasier syndrome?
questions.exp: The middle branch, Biopsy, lists focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. (Book p709)

questions.q: By which age does the Frasier diagram place renal failure?

questions.q: Which statement matches the WT2 section’s opening line?
opts: It is the ureteric-bud epithelial marker PAX-2
It is identified as a renal sodium channel
No role in epithelial–mesenchymal interaction is assigned here
It is the named driver of that interaction
questions.exp: The WT2 section opens with no role in epithelial mesenchymal interaction. “WT2” is the book’s historical locus/section label and should not be mistaken for a fully specified modern single-gene diagnosis. (Book p709)

questions.q: Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome is described as what type of anomaly?
questions.exp: The line beneath Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome reads genomic imprinting anomaly. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which tongue finding is illustrated in Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome?
questions.exp: The left photograph is captioned macroglossia. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which abdominal-wall finding is named in the middle Beckwith–Wiedemann photograph?
questions.exp: The middle photograph is captioned umbilical hernia. This is kept distinct from the later omphalocele bullet. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which renal size change is included in the organomegaly caption?
questions.exp: The organomegaly caption first lists nephromegaly; the ultrasound montage also labels bilateral nephromegaly. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which pair of enlarged abdominal organs is named next in the organomegaly caption?
questions.exp: The next listed finding is hepatosplenomegaly, meaning enlargement of the liver and spleen. (Book p709)

questions.q: Fill up: Enlargement of the adrenal glands in the organomegaly caption is termed ______.
questions.exp: The organomegaly caption ends with adrenomegaly. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which limb-growth finding is listed among the other Beckwith–Wiedemann features?
questions.exp: The first Others bullet is hemihypertrophy of limbs. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which abdominal-wall defect is separately listed under “Others”?
questions.exp: The second Others bullet is omphalocele; it is separate from the earlier umbilical-hernia photograph. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which childhood renal tumour is listed in Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome?
questions.exp: The next Others bullet is Wilms tumour. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which head-size term is actually printed in this book’s Beckwith–Wiedemann list?
questions.exp: The scan prints microcephaly. This is an atypical/questionable feature for Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome and is retained only as a flagged source claim, not promoted as a defining clinical diagnostic feature. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which ear finding follows the head-size term in the Beckwith–Wiedemann list?
questions.exp: The same bullet lists an ear-lobe crease after the slash. (Book p709)

questions.q: A newborn with Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome is screened for the glucose abnormality listed here. Which is it?
questions.exp: The next Others bullet is hypoglycaemia. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which adult renal association is listed for Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome?
questions.exp: The final Others bullet is medullary sponge kidney, with the qualifier in adults. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which facial shape is named for Russell Silver syndrome?
questions.exp: The first Russell Silver bullet is triangular facies. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which developmental feature does this book list beside triangular facies in Russell Silver syndrome?
questions.exp: The scan uses the historical wording “mental retardation.” This is recorded as a source claim, not as a universal feature or diagnostic requirement of Russell Silver syndrome; normal intellectual development can occur. (Book p709)

questions.q: Which sex predominance is printed for unilateral renal agenesis in this book?
questions.exp: The first bullet prints F > M. This question records the book’s epidemiological claim rather than asserting a universal sex distribution. (Book p710)

questions.q: What incidence does the book give for unilateral renal agenesis?
questions.exp: The second bullet prints 1 in 10,000 live births. This is a source-specific figure, not a claim that all epidemiological references agree. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which mutation is associated with unilateral renal agenesis in this section?
questions.exp: The next bullet lists PAX-2 mutation as an association; this does not mean every case has that mutation. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which ocular association is listed for unilateral renal agenesis?
questions.exp: The first association is optic nerve coloboma. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which cardiac-position abnormality is associated with unilateral renal agenesis here?
questions.exp: The next association is dextrocardia. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which blood-pressure abnormality is listed among these associations?
questions.exp: The next association is hypertension. (Book p710)

questions.q: What explanation is supplied for hypertension in unilateral renal agenesis?
questions.exp: The parenthetical explanation is decreased nephron number. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which foot abnormality completes the association list?
questions.exp: The final association is flat foot. (Book p710)

questions.q: Congenital absence of one kidney, the condition named by the upper imaging montage’s caption, is called:
questions.exp: The montage is captioned u/l renal agenesis. Its chest, abdominal, ultrasound and foot images accompany the unilateral association list; no additional unlabelled radiographic diagnosis is assumed. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which named syndrome is used for bilateral renal agenesis in this section?
questions.exp: Under Bilateral Renal Agenesis, the book uses Potter’s syndrome. Clinically, Potter sequence describes the effects of severe oligohydramnios and is not limited to one cause. (Book p710)

questions.q: The book calls Potter syndrome the “most common cause of death immediately after birth.” How should this be handled?
opts: Flag it as an unsupported broad source claim, not a universal mortality statistic
Accept it as the leading cause of every neonatal death worldwide
Infer that unilateral agenesis is invariably lethal
Infer that all affected infants have normal lung development
questions.exp: The sentence is present in the scan, but its unqualified “most common” claim should not be taught as an established universal neonatal mortality statistic. Bilateral renal agenesis can be lethal, notably through severe oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which gene is named in the RET/GDNF line under bilateral renal agenesis?
questions.exp: The line names RET gene / GDNF protein mutation. This records an association, not a claim that all bilateral agenesis is explained by RET. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which protein is paired with RET in the bilateral-agenesis line?
questions.exp: The protein named alongside RET is GDNF. (Book p710)

questions.q: What does GDNF stand for?
questions.exp: The scan abbreviates the expansion to “Glial derived neurotrophic factor.” The standard expansion is glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor. (Book p710)

questions.q: The Potter figure caption prints “pulmonary hyperplasia.” Which clinical interpretation is appropriate?
opts: Pulmonary hypoplasia; the printed caption appears erroneous
Pulmonary hyperplasia is the typical consequence
The caption proves that both lungs are absent
The caption means only transient neonatal tachypnoea
questions.exp: The actual caption says pulmonary hyperplasia. In Potter sequence the characteristic problem is pulmonary hypoplasia from severe oligohydramnios, not hyperplasia. The source error is made explicit rather than silently corrected or taught as clinical fact. (Book p710)

questions.q: What renal finding is named in the second Potter image caption?
questions.exp: The second caption begins absent kidney, within the bilateral renal agenesis section. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which vascular structures are also named as absent in that caption?
questions.exp: The same caption lists absent renal arteries after absent kidney. (Book p710)

questions.q: Which adrenal-gland shape is described in the final Potter image?
questions.exp: The last image is captioned disc shaped adrenal gland. (Book p710)

units.title: Mesoderm derivatives & urogenital system
units.guide: Source-order revision, 20 Sep 2026: questions have been expanded and reordered. Previous completion badges and XP are retained; replay this unit to cover the revised questions. Mesoderm splits into paraxial, intermediate and lateral plate derivatives. The lateral plate divides into somatopleure (outer serosal layers) and splanchnopleure (inner serosal layers). The urogenital system is built from intermediate mesoderm plus endoderm, which together form the cloaca.

units.title: Cloaca & urogenital sinus differentiation
units.guide: Source-order revision, 20 Sep 2026: questions have been expanded and reordered. Previous completion badges and XP are retained; replay this unit to cover the revised questions. The cloaca — the hindgut distal to the allantois — divides into the primitive urogenital sinus and the primitive rectum. The sinus's epithelial buds, vesicourethral canal and definitive urogenital sinus form the prostate, bladder and urethral segments, while the rectum carries the anal canal only up to the pectinate line, below which the canal is proctodermal.

units.title: Intermediate mesoderm: ducts & urogenital ridge
units.guide: Source-order revision, 20 Sep 2026: questions have been expanded and reordered. Previous completion badges and XP are retained; replay this unit to cover the revised questions. The intermediate mesoderm gives the Wolffian and Müllerian ducts and the urogenital ridge. The Wolffian duct throws off the ureteric bud that becomes the collecting system, while the ridge's medial genital ridge forms the gonads and its lateral nephrogenic cord forms the excretory part of the kidney. The metanephros is the permanent kidney.

units.title: Timeline of kidney development
units.guide: Source-order revision, 20 Sep 2026: questions have been expanded and reordered. Previous completion badges and XP are retained; replay this unit to cover the revised questions. The pronephros appears on day 22 and vanishes within days, the mesonephros by 4 months, and the metanephros is the permanent kidney. The first fully formed nephron appears by the end of week 8; nephrogenesis completes at 32–36 weeks with the nephron number fixed at birth, and urine concentration reaches adult level by 1.5 years.

units.title: CKD pathogenesis: nephron endowment
units.guide: Source-order revision, 20 Sep 2026: questions have been expanded and reordered. Previous completion badges and XP are retained; replay this unit to cover the revised questions. Birth weight defines the nephron number. Fewer functional nephrons force each nephron to hyperfilter — intraglomerular hypertension, capillary-pore stretching, albuminuria, tubular injury and TGF-β-driven fibrosis — ending in CKD with interstitial fibrosis, tubular atrophy and glomerulosclerosis.

units.title: Maternal factors, PAX-2 & kidney location
units.guide: Source-order revision, 20 Sep 2026: questions have been expanded and reordered. Previous completion badges and XP are retained; replay this unit to cover the revised questions. Maternal pre-eclampsia/hypertension produces placental insufficiency, IUGR and SGA offspring at risk of CKD, hypertension, hyperuricaemia, diabetes and metabolic syndrome. PAX-2 builds the ureteric bud epithelium, and the fetal kidney at S1–S2 sits below the adult T12–L3 level.
